title: The proem: 'Tell me, O Muse, of the man'
greek: ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, μοῦσα (andra moi ennepe, mousa)
short: The first word in Greek is 'man' (andra): the hero is announced but not named, and the Muse is asked to begin the tale wherever she chooses.
body: The Iliad opens with an emotion (mēnis, 'wrath'); the Odyssey opens with a person, andra, and keeps his name back until line 21. Ennepe ('tell') is the same verb as Latin insece, and Merry and Riddell note that Livius Andronicus, translating this line into Latin in the third century BC, wrote 'Virum mihi, Camena, insece versutum'. The proem names the hero's wanderings, the cities and minds he came to know, and his sufferings at sea. It then dwells, oddly, on a single episode, the comrades' eating of the Sun's cattle (Book 12), and says they died 'through their own blind folly'. That stress on human responsibility is taken up at once in Zeus' speech (1.32-43). The closing request, 'beginning where thou wilt' (amothen ge), leaves the Muse to choose the starting point; the poem then starts late, in the tenth year of Odysseus' return, the method Horace praised as plunging the hearer 'in medias res' (Ars Poetica 148).

title: Polytropos: 'of many devices' (or 'of many turns')
greek: πολύτροπον (polytropon)
short: Literally 'of many turns': either 'versatile, wily' or 'much turned about, much travelled'. Murray chooses the first sense; the ambiguity was debated already in antiquity.
body: The compound joins polys ('much') and tropos ('turn'). In Homer it occurs only here and at 10.330, where Circe uses it of Odysseus. Merry and Riddell take it as 'of many devices' (Latin versutus), because it matches the hero's other epithets, polymētis ('of many counsels'), polymēchanos ('of many resources') and poikilomētis ('of subtle mind'). Nitzsch, whom they report, read it passively as 'much-wandering', glossed by the clause that follows, 'who wandered full many ways'. The Homeric Hymn to Hermes gives the word to the trickster god (lines 13 and 439), which supports the active sense. Modern critics often think the poet wanted both senses: Odysseus is turned about by the sea and is himself a man of many turns of mind and speech. Pietro Pucci made the word the title and starting point of his study of the poem's self-conscious language.

title: Helios Hyperion (the Sun)
greek: Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο (Hyperionos Ēelioio)
short: Helios is the Sun god; 'Hyperion', literally 'he who goes above', is in Homer a title of the Sun himself, though Hesiod makes Hyperion his father.
body: The proem singles out one crime of the comrades: they ate the cattle of the Sun on the island of Thrinacia (told in Book 12), after being warned by Teiresias and Circe. Hyperion here is a by-name of Helios; at 1.24 it stands alone for the sun, 'where Hyperion sets'. In Hesiod's Theogony (371-374) Hyperion is a Titan and Helios his son, and the Odyssey once uses the patronymic form Hyperionidēs (12.176). Merry and Riddell argue that this need not be a true patronymic and report the view that Hyperion simply means 'the one on high'. The Sun, who 'sees all and hears all', is also a witness of oaths in Homer (Iliad 3.277), which helps explain why the offence against his herds is so severe.

title: Nostos: the return home
greek: νόστιμον ἦμαρ (nostimon ēmar); νόστος (nostos)
short: Nostos, 'homecoming', is the poem's central theme; the 'day of returning' is what the comrades lose and what Odysseus must win.
body: Odysseus strives for 'his own life and the return (nostos) of his comrades' (1.5), but the gods take from them 'the day of their returning'. The Odyssey belongs to a family of homecoming tales: a lost epic of the Trojan Cycle, the Nostoi ('Returns'), told the voyages of the other Greek leaders, and the Odyssey itself keeps comparing its hero's return with theirs. Phemius sings 'the woeful return of the Achaeans' (1.326-327); Nestor tells how the fleet split (Book 3); Menelaus tells of his own long detour through Egypt and of Agamemnon's murder on arrival (Book 4). Douglas Frame argued that nostos is related to noos ('mind') through a root meaning 'return to light and life', so that return and intelligence are bound together in Odysseus; the etymology is debated, but the pairing of the two words in 1.3-5 is striking.

title: Calypso, 'the Concealer', on Ogygia, 'the navel of the sea'
greek: νύμφη πότνι᾽ ἔρυκε Καλυψώ (numphē potni' eruke Kalupsō); ὀμφαλός … θαλάσσης (omphalos thalassēs, 1.50); Ὠγυγίη (Ōgugiē, 1.85)
short: Calypso's name comes from kalyptō, 'cover, hide': the nymph keeps Odysseus hidden on Ogygia, an island at 'the navel of the sea', far from any human route.
body: Calypso is a 'queenly nymph' living in hollow caves; her speaking name is formed from kalyptein, 'to cover, conceal', a verb Homer also uses of death covering the eyes. She wants Odysseus as husband and offers to make him immortal (5.135-136); his longing to see 'the smoke leaping up from his own land' (1.58-59) defines the human choice at the poem's heart, and his stay of seven years is given at 7.259. Athena places her island where 'is the navel (omphalos) of the sea', a phrase for utter remoteness, like the boss at the centre of a shield; later Greeks called Delphi the navel of the earth. The name Ogygia (1.85) recalls ōgygios, 'primeval'. Homer gives no real coordinates: Odysseus sails seventeen days to reach Scheria (5.278-280), and Merry and Riddell, at 1.85, refer the question of reconciling Homeric geography with fact to their note on 5.34. Ancient readers still tried: Plutarch puts an island Ogygia five days' sail west of Britain.

anchor: Ethiopians who dwell sundered in twain
title: The Ethiopians at the ends of the earth
greek: Αἰθίοπας τοὶ διχθὰ δεδαίαται, ἔσχατοι ἀνδρῶν (Aithiopas toi dichtha dedaiatai, eschatoi andrōn)
short: The 'Burnt-faced' people of the world's edge, divided between sunrise and sunset, with whom the gods feast; Poseidon's absence there frees the other gods to act.
body: Aithiops was understood as 'burnt-face' (aithō, 'burn', + ōps, 'face'). In Homer they are a pious, distant people beside the river Ocean, visited by gods for feasts (Zeus and the gods go to them at Iliad 1.423-424; Iris at Iliad 23.205-207). The 'farthermost of men' are split into two groups, one where the sun sets and one where it rises, which suits an early picture of a round earth ringed by Ocean, with the sun's path ending at both rims. Merry and Riddell compare Herodotus' later distinction between the Ethiopians above Egypt and the 'Eastern' Ethiopians (7.69-70). The narrative point is practical: with Poseidon away at his hecatomb, Athena can raise Odysseus' case before Zeus. Menelaus claims to have visited the Ethiopians in his wanderings (4.84).

title: Hecatomb
greek: ἑκατόμβη (hekatombē)
short: Literally a sacrifice of 'a hundred oxen'; in practice any great public sacrifice, here of bulls and rams.
body: The word combines hekaton ('hundred') and bous ('ox'), but Homer uses it loosely of any lavish offering, and here the victims are 'bulls and rams'. The gods are imagined as attending in person and 'taking joy' in the feast, a picture shared with the Iliad. The Odyssey gives two full sacrifice scenes in the books that follow: the Pylians' mass offering of black bulls to Poseidon on the beach (3.5-9) and Nestor's sacrifice of a heifer to Athena, described step by step (3.418-463). Menelaus is told that he was held in Egypt because he had not offered 'hecatombs that bring fulfilment' (4.352, 4.478-480), a reminder that failure to sacrifice is itself an offence. Walter Burkert's account of Greek sacrifice remains the standard modern guide to the ritual sequence.

title: 'Blameless' Aegisthus and the Oresteia story
greek: ἀμύμονος Αἰγίσθοιο (amymonos Aigisthoio)
short: Zeus calls the murderer Aegisthus amymōn, conventionally 'blameless'; the word marks rank or looks rather than morals. His story is the poem's recurring counter-model to Odysseus' homecoming.
body: Aegisthus seduced Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon, and killed Agamemnon on his return from Troy; seven years later Orestes killed him (3.303-310). That a man so condemned should be called amymōn troubled readers from antiquity on. Merry and Riddell explain the word as describing excellence of some kind, such as birth or beauty, 'almost titular, like our epithet gallant', and not moral praise. Anne Amory Parry's monograph Blameless Aegisthus made the same case at length. The story is told again and again in Books 1-4 (1.35-43, 1.298-300, 3.193-200, 3.254-312, 4.512-537) and returns in the Underworld (11.405-434) and at the end (24.192-202). It sets up a contrast: Agamemnon, Clytemnestra and Orestes against Odysseus, Penelope and Telemachus. Telemachus is urged to act like Orestes, and the reader is invited to fear that Odysseus will meet Agamemnon's fate.

anchor: mortals are to blame the gods
title: Zeus' complaint: human folly and divine justice
greek: ὢ πόποι, οἷον δή νυ θεοὺς βροτοὶ αἰτιόωνται (ō popoi, hoion dē nu theous brotoi aitioōntai)
short: The poem's first divine speech: men blame the gods, but by their own reckless folly (atasthaliai) they suffer 'beyond what is ordained'.
body: Zeus says mortals bring sorrows on themselves 'beyond their lot' (hyper moron) through atasthaliai, 'reckless wickedness' (Murray's 'blind folly'), the same word the proem used of the comrades (1.7). Aegisthus is the proof: the gods warned him through Hermes and he went ahead. The speech is often read as programmatic. The suitors will also be warned (by Halitherses at 2.161-176, by the disguised Odysseus to Amphinomus at 18.125-150) and will die 'through their own wickedness' (22.416). Hugh Lloyd-Jones used the passage to argue for a coherent idea of divine justice running from Homer onward. Others point out that the poem does not apply it consistently: Poseidon persecutes Odysseus for a deed done in self-defence, and the Phaeacians are punished for their hospitality. Jenny Strauss Clay reads the speech against Athena's reply, which turns the conversation at once to Odysseus.

title: Hermes Argeiphontes
greek: ἐύσκοπον ἀργεϊφόντην (euskopon argeiphontēn)
short: A title of Hermes, the gods' messenger, of uncertain meaning; the ancient explanation 'slayer of Argus' is only one of several.
body: Hermes is the gods' envoy in the Odyssey: he warned Aegisthus, and Athena now proposes sending him to Calypso (1.84-87; he goes in Book 5). Argeiphontēs is one of his commonest titles but its meaning was already lost to the Greeks. The scholia offered several guesses, the most popular being 'slayer of Argus', the hundred-eyed watchman whom Hermes killed to free Io. Merry and Riddell reject this as a later invention to explain an obscure word; they connect the first part with argos, 'bright', and suggest either 'brightly appearing' or 'sky-clearing'. Modern scholars remain divided, and LSJ records the ancient alternatives. Euskopos, 'keen-sighted' or 'watchful', also fits a god who guards flocks and travellers.

title: Glaukōpis Athena, 'flashing-eyed'
greek: γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη (glaukōpis Athēnē)
short: Athena's standing epithet: probably 'with gleaming eyes'; the link some make with glaux, 'owl', is possible but not certain.
body: The compound joins glaukos, 'gleaming, pale bluish-grey', with ōps, 'eye, face'. Merry and Riddell argue that the idea is brightness rather than colour, comparing the terrible flashing of Athena's eyes in Iliad 1.200, and they cite a scholiast who derives the word from glaussein, 'to shine'. A much-repeated alternative is 'owl-eyed', since the owl (glaux) was Athena's bird at Athens; most lexicographers treat this as a secondary association rather than the original meaning. Athena dominates Books 1-4: she pleads for Odysseus in heaven, then takes human form as Mentes and Mentor to guide Telemachus. Her favour to Odysseus contrasts with her anger against the returning Achaeans (1.326-327, 3.135).

anchor: daughter of Atlas of baneful mind
title: Atlas 'of baneful mind'
greek: Ἄτλαντος θυγάτηρ ὀλοόφρονος (Atlantos thugatēr oloophronos)
short: Calypso's father Atlas knows the depths of every sea and holds the pillars that keep earth and sky apart; 'baneful-minded' marks his dangerous, uncanny knowledge.
body: In Hesiod (Theogony 517-520) Atlas stands at the ends of the earth near the Hesperides and holds up the sky himself, by the will of Zeus; the Odyssey has him keeping the 'tall pillars' that hold earth and heaven apart. The epithet oloophrōn, 'of destructive mind', is used in the Odyssey of other wizard-like figures, Aeetes (10.137) and Minos (11.322). Merry and Riddell explain it from his superhuman knowledge of the sea's depths: such knowledge makes its owner feared. They also report two older theories, one linking the epithet to Atlas' part in the Titans' revolt, and one, by Nägelsbach, reading Atlas and Calypso as memories of Phoenician traders who kept the western sea routes secret. Proteus, 'who knows the depths of every sea' (4.385-386), is described in the same words.

title: Poseidon 'earth-enfolder' and 'earth-shaker'
greek: Ποσειδάων γαιήοχος (Poseidaōn gaiēochos); ἐννοσίγαιος (ennosigaios, 1.74)
short: Two standing titles of Poseidon: gaiēochos, of disputed meaning ('earth-holder' or 'earth-embracer'), and ennosigaios, 'earth-shaker', god of earthquakes as well as the sea.
body: Merry and Riddell note that the older commentators explained gaiēochos as 'earth-surrounding', since the sea encircles the land; because ochos ('holding') is hard to take in that sense, others proposed 'earth-supporting' or simply 'lord of the earth'. Ennosigaios (and the variant enosichthōn, 3.6) is clearer: Poseidon shakes the ground, and Greeks attributed earthquakes to him. He is also 'dark-haired' (3.6) and lord of horses. In the Odyssey he is Odysseus' divine enemy, angry 'because of the Cyclops' (1.69), whose blinding and Polyphemus' prayer for vengeance are told in Book 9 (9.526-536). Zeus' assurance that Poseidon 'will let go his anger' because he cannot fight all the other gods (1.77-79) sets the terms of the plot.

title: Polyphemus the Cyclops
greek: ἀντίθεον Πολύφημον (antitheon Polyphēmon)
short: The one-eyed giant son of Poseidon whom Odysseus blinded (Book 9); his name means 'much-spoken-of' or 'many-voiced'.
body: Polyphēmos is formed from polys ('much') and phēmē ('speech, report'), so 'famous' or 'loud-voiced'. The poet calls him 'godlike' (antitheos), a conventional epithet of rank that sits ironically on a cannibal. His mother is the nymph Thoosa, daughter of Phorcys, an old sea god. The blinding is the root of Poseidon's grudge, and Book 9 will show how Odysseus provoked it by shouting his real name as he sailed away. Book 2 adds a grim detail: the Cyclops ate Antiphus, son of the Ithacan elder Aegyptius (2.17-20). Merry and Riddell's appendix surveys folk-tale versions of the blinded giant from many cultures, an approach developed by later folklorists.

title: 'The long-haired Achaeans'
greek: κάρη κομόωντας Ἀχαιούς (karē komoōntas Achaious)
short: A formulaic name for the Greeks: 'Achaeans' (with 'Argives' and 'Danaans') is Homer's word for the Greeks as a whole, and long hair marked free men of standing.
body: Merry and Riddell explain Achaioi as properly the name of the dominant tribe of northern Greece and the Peloponnese, extended to the whole Greek people; in the Odyssey it includes the Ithacans themselves (1.394, 2.7). The phrase karē komoōntas, 'wearing the hair long on the head', is a fixed formula at the end of the verse. They compare the Abantes of Iliad 2.542, who let their hair grow at the back. Long hair seems to have marked warriors and free men; cutting the hair was a sign of mourning (4.198). The formula appears here in Athena's plan that Telemachus should call an assembly, which he does at the start of Book 2.

anchor: Mentes, the leader of the Taphians
title: Mentes, lord of the Taphians: Athena's first disguise
greek: εἰδομένη ξείνῳ, Ταφίων ἡγήτορι Μέντῃ (eidomenē xeinōi, Taphiōn hēgētori Mentēi)
short: Athena takes the shape of Mentes, a guest-friend of the family and chief of the seafaring Taphians, a trader carrying iron to exchange for copper.
body: Merry and Riddell place the Taphians in the islets off Leucas, the largest being Taphos (modern Meganisi), and note that they had a name for piracy; Homer calls them 'oar-loving' (1.181). Mentes says he is sailing 'to men of strange speech, on my way to Temese for copper' with a cargo of iron (1.183-184). Strabo located Temese (Tempsa) in south Italy, but Merry and Riddell prefer Tamassos in Cyprus, famous for copper mines. The name Mentes, like Mentor, the second figure Athena impersonates, is built on the root men- ('mind, spirit, force'), and Athena's task is to put menos ('courage') in Telemachus (1.321). Merry and Riddell point out that the Greek eidomenē means real bodily likeness, not mere resemblance.

title: Xenia: guest-friendship and the welcome of a stranger
greek: νεμεσσήθη δ᾽ ἐνὶ θυμῷ ξεῖνον δηθὰ θύρῃσιν ἐφεστάμεν (nemessēthē d' eni thymōi xeinon dētha thurēisin ephestamen)
short: Telemachus is indignant that a stranger stands waiting at the door; his welcome follows the ritual order of Homeric hospitality, food first and questions after.
body: Xenos means both 'stranger' and 'guest-friend', and the bond of xenia, protected by Zeus Xenios, is a central value of the poem. Telemachus feels nemesis (righteous indignation) at the neglect: he takes the guest's hand and spear, greets him ('Hail, stranger', chaire xeine), seats him on a fine chair apart from the noisy suitors, has water brought for washing, and serves food; only then does he ask who the stranger is (1.123-124, 1.169-177). Steve Reece analysed such hospitality scenes into a fixed sequence of elements, and M. W. Edwards studied them as type-scenes. The contrast is pointed: the suitors are themselves abusing hospitality by feasting uninvited, and the poem tests every host by how he treats strangers, from Nestor and Menelaus to the Cyclops and the suitors' treatment of the disguised Odysseus. The exchange of gifts that seals xenia is promised at 1.311-318.

title: 'Winged words'
greek: ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα (epea pteroenta prosēuda)
short: The most famous Homeric speech formula: words that fly, like birds or feathered arrows, from speaker to hearer.
body: The line 'and he spoke, and addressed her with winged words' introduces speeches throughout both epics. Merry and Riddell report Classen's count of forty-four uses of the full line with phōnēsas, and his finding that it marks the start of a speech, the resumption of one, or a solemn or emphatic utterance. The image of the 'winged' word has been explained either from birds in flight or from the feathers that guide an arrow, so that speech travels swiftly and surely to its target. The formula is one of the best examples of what Milman Parry called the economy of Homeric diction: a ready-made phrase that fills a fixed part of the hexameter. Murray translates it the same way almost every time, so English readers can see its regularity.

title: Phemius, the bard who 'sang perforce', and his song of the Return
greek: Φημίῳ, ὅς ῥ᾽ ἤειδε παρὰ μνηστῆρσιν ἀνάγκῃ (Phēmiōi, hos rh' ēeide para mnēstērsin anankēi); Ἀχαιῶν νόστον … λυγρόν (Achaiōn noston … lugron, 1.326-327)
short: Phemius ('Man of Report') is the Ithacan singer forced to entertain the suitors; his song of the Achaeans' bitter return from Troy brings Penelope down in tears.
body: Song and dance are 'the crown of a feast' (1.152), and Phemius sings 'perforce' (anankēi), a detail that saves him in Book 22, where he pleads that he is self-taught and sang under compulsion (22.344-356). His name, from phēmē ('report, fame'), suits a man who spreads kleos. His subject here is 'the woeful return of the Achaeans, which Pallas Athena laid upon them'. Merry and Riddell note that everything Phemius and Demodocus sing comes from the Trojan saga (except the song of Ares and Aphrodite), so that the war has become recent history; the lay seems to be one episode from the cycle of 'returns'. Athena's anger arose from the Locrian Ajax's outrage on Cassandra (3.135, 4.499-511). The irony is rich: the goddess who caused the disaster sits disguised in the hall, and the song concerns the very return Penelope longs for. Phemius and Demodocus (Book 8) give the Odyssey a picture of epic performance within the epic.

title: 'The wine-dark sea'
greek: οἴνοπα πόντον (oinopa ponton)
short: Oinops, literally 'wine-faced' or 'wine-looking', is a fixed epithet of the sea (and of oxen); whether it means a colour or a sheen is uncertain.
body: Merry and Riddell note that the word may mean 'glittering', like aithops, an epithet of wine itself, though the older commentators, following Eustathius, took it as 'dark', since ancient wine was dark. W. E. Gladstone's Studies on Homer (1858) used this and similar epithets to argue that Homer's colour vocabulary was very unlike ours, a claim much discussed since. Most modern readers take the epithet to evoke the deep dark sheen of the open sea rather than a hue we could match exactly. It appears again when the west wind sings 'over the wine-dark sea' at Telemachus' departure (2.421).

title: Telemachus' doubt: 'no man knows his own parentage'
greek: οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω (ou gar pō tis heon gonon autos anegnō)
short: Telemachus' guarded reply, 'my mother says I am his child, but I know not', is proverbial caution, not a slur on Penelope; it opens the theme of the true son.
body: The remark is proverbial in form: no one can know his own begetting at first hand. It shows Telemachus' insecurity in a house without a father, and the poem answers it repeatedly. Athena (as Mentes) remarks on his likeness to Odysseus' head and eyes (1.208-209); as Mentor she says few sons are like their fathers (2.276-277); Nestor is amazed that his speech is like his father's (3.123-125); Helen and Menelaus recognize him by his likeness (4.141-154). The question is less paternity than worth: will he prove an heir fit for Odysseus? De Jong notes how these recognitions mark the stages of his growth through the Telemachy.

title: Feast, wedding or eranos?
greek: εἰλαπίνη ἠὲ γάμος; ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἔρανος τάδε γ᾽ ἐστίν (eilapinē ēe gamos; epei ouk eranos tade g' estin)
short: Athena names three kinds of feast: one host's banquet, a wedding, and an eranos held at each member's house in turn. The suitors' feasting is none of these.
body: Merry and Riddell explain that the eranos was a club meal whose mark was that it moved from house to house, as Telemachus demands when he tells the suitors to feast 'eating your own substance and changing from house to house' (1.374-375). The eilapinē was a lavish feast given by a single host; the gamos was a wedding feast, provided by the bride's family. The three appear together again at 11.415. The suitors' gatherings fit no category: they feast at one man's expense, without his consent, and without end. Athena's question thus defines their crime in social terms, as an abuse of the forms of commensality, before Telemachus describes it in moral ones.

anchor: on the knees of the gods
title: 'These things lie on the knees of the gods'
greek: ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται (tauta theōn en gounasi keitai)
short: A formula for an outcome that rests with the gods and that human wishing cannot decide.
body: The phrase is used again by Eurymachus (1.400) and in the Iliad (17.514, 20.435). Its image is debated. One ancient explanation links it to suppliants clasping the knees of gods or to offerings laid on the knees of cult statues. Merry and Riddell reject this and also Nitzsch's view that the knees are the seat of strength; they suggest instead the image of judges or umpires who hold the prizes on their knees until the contest is decided, comparing a proverb 'it lies on the knees of five judges'. On any reading, the formula sets human planning against divine decision, just as Athena urges Telemachus to act while leaving the result to the gods.

anchor: make ready the gifts full many
title: Marriage gifts (hedna): who gives them?
greek: οἱ δὲ γάμον τεύξουσι καὶ ἀρτυνέουσιν ἔεδνα (hoi de gamon teuxousi kai artynousin eedna)
short: Athena says that if Penelope remarries, her father's household will prepare the wedding and 'the gifts'; Homer's marriage-gift customs here seem inconsistent and have been much argued over.
body: Usually in Homer the suitor gives hedna (often cattle) to the bride's family to win her (16.390-392, 11.282), and the suitors themselves speak of doing so. Here, and in Eurymachus' repetition (2.196-197), the bride's family prepares hedna 'such as should follow a well-loved daughter', which sounds like a dowry. Merry and Riddell, reporting Nitzsch, reject the idea that hedna here means a dowry and suggest that the hedna received from the groom were, at least in part, used by the bride's family to provide her outfit and feast, and so returned in a different form; they admit that this solution seems forced. M. I. Finley treated marriage in the poems as a form of gift exchange; A. M. Snodgrass argued that the inconsistencies show the epic mixing customs from different periods rather than describing one real society.

anchor: what fame the goodly Orestes won
title: Kleos and the example of Orestes
greek: ἢ οὐκ ἀΐεις οἷον κλέος ἔλλαβε δῖος Ὀρέστης (ē ouk aieis hoion kleos ellabe dios Orestēs)
short: Athena urges Telemachus to win kleos, 'fame', as Orestes did by killing his father's murderer; Orestes is held up as the model son.
body: Kleos is literally 'what is heard' (from kluein, 'to hear'): reputation carried by report and song. It is the reward heroes seek, and Gregory Nagy's work made it central to modern readings of epic. Telemachus' journey is meant partly to gain him 'good report among men' (1.95, 3.78). Orestes is the explicit model, cited by Athena here and again by Nestor (3.196-200); in each telling the Odyssey stresses the revenge on Aegisthus and passes over the matricide, alluding to Clytemnestra only as Orestes' 'hateful mother' at the funeral feast (3.310). Scholars such as S. D. Olson have shown how the poem selects from the Oresteia story to fit its own situation. Orestes 'came back from Athens' in Nestor's account (3.307), a variant that troubled ancient critics.

title: Athena departs 'as a bird' (anopaia)
greek: ὄρνις δ᾽ ὣς ἀνόπαια διέπτατο (ornis d' hōs anopaia dieptato)
short: Athena leaves 'like a bird'; the rare word anopaia was read in antiquity as 'upward', 'unseen', 'through the smoke-hole', or as the name of a bird.
body: Merry and Riddell set out the ancient interpretations recorded by Apollonius the lexicographer: some took anopaia as a species of bird (a kind of sea-eagle), others as 'invisibly', others as 'up through the opening' in the roof. They argue that ornis hōs is a compressed simile, not a literal transformation, comparing Odysseus clinging to the fig tree 'like a bat' (12.433). The question matters because elsewhere Athena seems actually to take bird form, as at 3.372, where she leaves Pylos 'in the likeness of a sea-eagle', and at 22.240, as a swallow. Murray's 'flying upward' follows one ancient view. Whatever the detail, Telemachus realizes that his visitor was a god (1.322-323), and the encounter changes him.

title: Penelope's veil (krēdemnon)
greek: ἄντα παρειάων σχομένη λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα (anta pareiaōn schomenē lipara krēdemna)
short: Penelope appears among the suitors standing by the door-post, veil drawn across her cheeks, flanked by two maids: a fixed scene of modest, guarded public appearance.
body: The krēdemnon (from kara, 'head', and deō, 'bind') was, Merry and Riddell suggest, a head-cloth tied with a band, with flaps that could be drawn across the face. Penelope holds it 'before her face'. The whole tableau, her descent from the upper room, her place by the pillar of the hall, the veil and the two attendants, recurs with small variations whenever she confronts the suitors (16.414-416, 18.208-211, 21.63-66). It signals chastity and status and also shows how her appearance itself stirs the suitors (1.365-366). Marilyn Katz and others have studied how such scenes construct Penelope's ambiguous position, at once desired, wise, and constrained.

title: 'The newest song' and 'speech shall be for men': Telemachus asserts authority
greek: ἥ τις ἀκουόντεσσι νεωτάτη ἀμφιπέληται (hē tis akouontessi neōtatē amphipelētai, 1.352); μῦθος δ᾽ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει πᾶσι, μάλιστα δ᾽ ἐμοί (muthos d' andressi melēsei pasi, malista d' emoi, 1.358-359)
short: Telemachus defends the bard (men praise most the newest song) and sends Penelope back to her loom with words adapted from Hector: 'war' in the Iliad becomes 'speech' here.
body: Telemachus argues that the singer is not to blame for his subject, since Zeus allots good and ill to men, and that audiences praise most 'the song which comes the newest to their ears' (1.351-352), one of the earliest Greek statements about poetic taste; Plato quotes it when warning against novelty in music (Republic 4.424b-c). He then repeats almost word for word Hector's farewell to Andromache (Iliad 6.490-493), sending her to 'the loom and the distaff', but where Hector said 'war shall be for men', Telemachus says mythos, 'speech', and adds 'most of all for me; since mine is the authority in the house'. The change suits Ithaca, where the struggle is first one of words. Penelope is amazed and obeys (1.360), a sign that her son is coming of age; the lines recur at 21.350-353 before the contest of the bow. Merry and Riddell explain 'ply' (epoichesthai) as walking to and fro at the upright loom, and 'chamber' as the women's quarters.

title: Antinous and Eurymachus, leaders of the suitors
greek: Ἀντίνοος … Εὐπείθεος υἱός (Antinoos … Eupeitheos huios)
short: The two chief suitors are introduced: Antinous, violent and contemptuous, and Eurymachus, son of Polybus, smooth and deceitful. Their names are telling.
body: Antinoos can be read as 'opposite-minded' or 'hostile in mind' (anti + noos); his father Eupeithes is 'Good Persuader'. Eurymachus means 'wide-fighting'. Speaking names of this kind are common among the Odyssey's minor characters, and their interpretation is often uncertain; von Kamptz's study of Homeric personal names and Carolyn Higbie's work discuss the evidence. Antinous is the more brutal: he sneers at Telemachus here and in the assembly, plots to murder him (4.660-672), and throws a footstool at the beggar Odysseus (17.462-465); he is the first suitor killed (22.8-21). Eurymachus speaks gently but plans the same ends, and Penelope's later speeches show she sees through both. Eupeithes leads the families' revenge in Book 24.

title: Eurycleia, the old nurse
greek: Εὐρύκλει᾽, Ὦπος θυγάτηρ Πεισηνορίδαο … ἐεικοσάβοια δ᾽ ἔδωκεν (Euryklei', Ōpos thugatēr Peisēnoridao … eeikosaboia d' edōken)
short: Laertes bought Eurycleia as a young girl for the price of twenty oxen; she nursed Odysseus and Telemachus and is the household's most trusted servant.
body: Her name means 'Wide Fame'. Value in Homer is often counted in oxen: Merry and Riddell note that twenty oxen was a high price, comparing Iliad 23.705, where a skilled woman is valued at four. Laertes honoured her 'as his faithful wife' but never slept with her, for fear of his wife's anger, a detail that contrasts with Agamemnon's treatment of captive women and fits the poem's interest in marital loyalty. Eurycleia is the keeper of the storeroom (2.345-347), keeps Telemachus' secret (2.373-380, 4.742-749), and in Book 19 recognizes Odysseus by the scar on his leg while washing his feet. Her careful folding of Telemachus' tunic at the end of this book closes the first day of the poem on a quiet domestic note.
